mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding hide tooth decay underneath?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding can potentially conceal early signs of decay, which is why regular dental examinations remain essential. While bonding creates a protective barrier, decay can still develop at the margins or beneath damaged areas of the restoration. Professional assessment using clinical examination and radiographs can detect hidden decay that may not be visible to patients.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding typically last before needing replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding generally lasts between 3-7 years, depending on factors such as oral hygiene, diet, habits, and the location of the bonding. Bonding on back teeth typically experiences more wear due to chewing forces. The underlying tooth health significantly impacts longevity, as damage to the natural tooth structure often necessitates earlier replacement regardless of the bonding's condition.

mainEntity.name: Is it painful to replace composite bonding when the tooth is damaged?

acceptedAnswer.text: The replacement procedure itself is typically comfortable, as local anaesthetic can be used when necessary. However, if underlying tooth damage involves decay reaching the nerve or structural fractures, additional treatment may be required which could involve more extensive procedures. Many patients find the procedure comfortable when appropriate local anaesthetic is used.

mainEntity.name: Can I prevent damage to the tooth under composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, maintaining excellent oral hygiene, avoiding hard foods and harmful habits like nail biting, and attending regular dental check-ups significantly reduce the risk of underlying tooth damage. Using fluoride toothpaste helps strengthen tooth enamel, while avoiding excessive sugar and acid helps prevent decay around bonded areas.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I ignore symptoms of damage under my bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ignoring symptoms can lead to more extensive damage requiring complex treatments such as crowns, root canal therapy, or even tooth extraction in severe cases. Early intervention when symptoms first appear typically results in simpler, less costly treatments and better long-term outcomes for both the tooth and any replacement restoration.

mainEntity.name: Will insurance cover replacement of composite bonding due to tooth damage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Coverage varies depending on your specific insurance plan and the reason for replacement. Treatment for underlying tooth damage such as decay or fractures is often covered, while purely cosmetic replacement may not be. It's advisable to check with your insurance provider regarding coverage for your specific situation and treatment needs.
